content: The Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, commonly referred to as the Dunedin Longitudinal Study, is an extensive cohort study that has been ongoing for several decades. It involves 1,037 individuals who were born within a one-year period in Dunedin, New Zealand, between April 1, 1972, and March 31, 1973. These individuals were selected for the study if they were still residing in the Otago region three years after their birth. Participants in the study were first assessed at the age of three, and subsequent assessments were conducted at ages 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 26, and most recently at age 32. Future assessments are planned for ages 38, 44, and 50. During each assessment, participants are brought back to Dunedin from wherever they are living globally. They undergo a comprehensive evaluation process that includes interviews, physical examinations, dental assessments, blood tests, computer-based questionnaires, and surveys. In addition to the primary study, spin-off studies have been conducted to gather data on the parents of the original participants and, since 2007, on the children of the original cohort. This approach allows researchers to collect information spanning three generations within the same families. The study places a strong emphasis on retaining participants, achieving an exceptional retention rate. At the most recent assessment at age 32, 96% of all living eligible participants, or 972 individuals, took part. This retention rate is remarkable compared to other longitudinal studies, which often experience dropout rates of 20-40%. The data collected from this study has generated a vast repository of information on various aspects of human health and development. Over 1,000 academic papers, reports, book chapters, and other publications have been produced using findings from the study. The multidisciplinary nature of the study has been a central focus, with data encompassing a wide range of health domains, including: Cardiovascular health and associated risk factors Respiratory health Oral health Sexual and reproductive health Mental health Psychosocial functioning Other health areas, such as sensory, musculoskeletal, and digestive health In 1996, a book titled From Child to Adult: Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study was published to present the major findings of the study in a format accessible to non-specialists. However, this book only includes information up to the age-21 assessment. Future plans for the Dunedin Study include the publication of another popular science book, enhancements to their website to make it more appealing and accessible to non-specialists, and the introduction of additional resources aimed at engaging the general public.
